Real and complex symplectic normal forms of functions

A canonical coordinate change preserves Poisson brackets. Multiplication by a nonzero function gives additional freedom, and for a complex symbol that freedom can remove an entire sequence of transverse errors. We develop the local models, including the exact marked covector, the homogeneity of every multiplier, and the distinction between a simple bracket and fixed higher contact.

We retain the conventions and geometry of Phase space and generating families, the nonzero restricted primitive theorem in Homogeneous submanifold normal forms, and the full coordinate completion in Prescribed canonical coordinates and isotropic fibers. The exact prerequisites are finite-coordinate flows, NF1–NF7, tangent and commuting flows, F0–F1, and inverse and implicit functions, P2–P3. The measure and norm proofs, M3–M8 give Fatou, dominated convergence, product integration, completeness and smooth density; Fourier proofs L1–L3 give the actual inverse maps, distributional compatibility and measurable multipliers. B1–B2 prove the weighted Fourier norms and their local frequency estimate. The proof map supplies exact locators and all earlier inputs. Section 4 proves smooth division by a complex function of one real variable, using an almost-analytic extension and a smooth complex root. The geometric source is Hörmander III, Section 21.3, Theorems 21.3.1–21.3.6, including the proof ending on; the division theorem is credited to Hörmander I, Theorem 7.5.6. These are the exact approved purchased editions; their use and ordinary citations are valid. The present proof supplies the needed one-variable division and parameter solver.

Our changes are multiplication p↦app\mapsto app↦ap by a nowhere zero smooth homogeneous complex function and a local homogeneous canonical map χ\chiχ, with the convention that χ\chiχ carries model coordinates to a neighborhood of ccc. All conclusions are local conic germs. The multiplier can change degree: if ppp has degree mmm, multiplying by ∣ξ∣1−m|\xi|^{1-m}∣ξ∣1−m makes it degree one.

Theorem 1.1 (real principal-type model). Suppose ppp is real, smooth and homogeneous of degree one, p(c)=0p(c)=0p(c)=0, and Hp(c)H_p(c)Hp​(c) and R(c)R(c)R(c) are independent. There are homogeneous canonical coordinates, with ccc represented by (0,en)(0,e_n)(0,en​), such that

χ∗p=ξ1.(1.3) \chi^*p=\xi_1. \tag{1.3} χ∗p=ξ1​.(1.3)

Proof. Prescribe the degree-one momentum p1=pp_1=pp1​=p, no position coordinates, and the marked values pj(c)=δjnp_j(c)=\delta_{jn}pj​(c)=δjn​, qj(c)=0q_j(c)=0qj​(c)=0. The homogeneous coordinate-completion theorem applies precisely because the given Hamilton field and RRR are independent. Its unused position index is nnn, whose prescribed momentum is nonzero. The completed coordinate map has the stated mark and retains ppp as an actual function. Its inverse is χ\chiχ. □\square□

The hypothesis includes the marked compatibility. In dimension one it cannot hold at a zero: dp(R)=p=0dp(R)=p=0dp(R)=p=0, so HpH_pHp​ and RRR lie in the same one-dimensional symplectic orthogonal. For example p=xξp=x\xip=xξ near (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) has Hp=−RH_p=-RHp​=−R at its zero. A homogeneous transformation could not turn this zero into the model momentum at (0,e1)(0,e_1)(0,e1​), where that momentum equals one.

If a real symbol initially has degree mmm, the positive preliminary multiplier scales its Hamilton field at a zero by a positive number, so it preserves nonradiality and gives (1.3) for the multiplied symbol.

3. A nonzero complex bracket and its marked sign

Write p=p1+ip2p=p_1+ip_2p=p1​+ip2​, with real pjp_jpj​. At a zero of ppp, every derivative of a scalar multiplier aaa is accompanied by a factor ppp or pˉ\bar ppˉ​, so

{Re⁡(ap),Im⁡(ap)}=∣a∣2{p1,p2}on p=0.(3.1) \{\operatorname{Re}(ap),\operatorname{Im}(ap)\} =|a|^2\{p_1,p_2\}\quad\hbox{on }p=0. \tag{3.1} {Re(ap),Im(ap)}=∣a∣2{p1​,p2​}on p=0.(3.1)

The sign of a nonzero bracket is therefore invariant under our changes.

We first supply the homogeneous auxiliary momentum used in this and the higher-contact construction.

Lemma 3.1 (a commuting positive momentum). Suppose ϕ,ψ\phi,\psiϕ,ψ are real homogeneous functions of degrees a,ba,ba,b, a+b=1a+b=1a+b=1, ϕ(c)=ψ(c)=0\phi(c)=\psi(c)=0ϕ(c)=ψ(c)=0, and {ϕ,ψ}=1\{\phi,\psi\}=1{ϕ,ψ}=1. There is a positive degree-one function hhh, with h(c)=1h(c)=1h(c)=1, such that

{ϕ,h}={ψ,h}=0.(3.2) \{\phi,h\}=\{\psi,h\}=0. \tag{3.2} {ϕ,h}={ψ,h}=0.(3.2)

Moreover

P=hbϕ,Q=h−bψ,h(3.3) P=h^b\phi,\qquad Q=h^{-b}\psi,\qquad h \tag{3.3} P=hbϕ,Q=h−bψ,h(3.3)

can be retained as the first momentum, first position and last momentum of a homogeneous canonical coordinate system with mark (0,en)(0,e_n)(0,en​).

Proof. The fields Hϕ,HψH_\phi,H_\psiHϕ​,Hψ​ commute because their bracket is the Hamilton field of the constant one. Their span is symplectic: ω(Hϕ,Hψ)={ϕ,ψ}=1\omega(H_\phi,H_\psi)=\{\phi,\psi\}=1ω(Hϕ​,Hψ​)={ϕ,ψ}=1. The zero set Z={ϕ=ψ=0}Z=\{\phi=\psi=0\}Z={ϕ=ψ=0} is a transverse section for their two commuting flows. The radial field lies in TZTZTZ, and is nonzero there. Choose a positive degree-one function h0h_0h0​ on ZZZ, equal to one at ccc, by using a transverse section to its radial flow and extending its positive datum.

The product of the two Hamilton flows from ZZZ is a local diffeomorphism. Extend h0h_0h0​ constantly in both flow times. This proves (3.2), positivity and the marked value. Dilations carry each flow to the same flow with a rescaled time, because of (1.2), and carry ZZZ to itself. The extension of t−1δt∗ht^{-1}\delta_t^*ht−1δt∗​h has the same datum and the same two zero transport equations as hhh. Flow uniqueness proves its equality to hhh. Thus hhh has degree one.

The product rule in (3.3) gives

{P,Q}=1,{P,h}={Q,h}=0,deg⁡P=1,deg⁡Q=0.(3.4) \{P,Q\}=1,\qquad \{P,h\}=\{Q,h\}=0,\qquad \deg P=1,\quad\deg Q=0. \tag{3.4} {P,Q}=1,{P,h}={Q,h}=0,degP=1,degQ=0.(3.4)

At ccc, HP=HϕH_P=H_\phiHP​=Hϕ​, HQ=HψH_Q=H_\psiHQ​=Hψ​. The field HhH_hHh​ is orthogonal to their symplectic span and nonzero, since dh(R)=h=1dh(R)=h=1dh(R)=h=1. If RRR were in the span of these three fields, pairing with HP,HQH_P,H_QHP​,HQ​ would force its first two coefficients to vanish. Then RRR would be a multiple of HhH_hHh​, contradicting dh(R)=1dh(R)=1dh(R)=1 and dh(Hh)=0dh(H_h)=0dh(Hh​)=0. Hence the three prescribed Hamilton fields and RRR are independent. The homogeneous coordinate theorem applies with Q=q1Q=q_1Q=q1​, P=p1P=p_1P=p1​, h=pnh=p_nh=pn​, and the unused position index nnn, whose momentum value is one. It completes the coordinates and preserves these functions exactly. □\square□

Theorem 3.2 (simple complex normal form). Let ppp be smooth and homogeneous near ccc, p(c)=0p(c)=0p(c)=0, and {p1,p2}(c)≠0\{p_1,p_2\}(c)\ne0{p1​,p2​}(c)=0. There is a nonzero homogeneous multiplier aaa and a homogeneous canonical map such that

First make the degree one by a positive multiplier, which preserves the bracket sign at the zero. In the positive case apply Theorem 2.1 with weights 1/2,1/21/2,1/21/2,1/2. Then

ϕ=u1/2p1,ψ=u1/2p2,{ϕ,ψ}=1,deg⁡ϕ=deg⁡ψ=12.(3.6) \phi=u^{1/2}p_1,\qquad \psi=u^{1/2}p_2,\qquad \{\phi,\psi\}=1,\qquad\deg\phi=\deg\psi=\tfrac12. \tag{3.6} ϕ=u1/2p1​,ψ=u1/2p2​,{ϕ,ψ}=1,degϕ=degψ=21​.(3.6)

h1/2u1/2p=η1+iy1ηn.(3.8) h^{1/2}u^{1/2}p=\eta_1+i y_1\eta_n. \tag{3.8} h1/2u1/2p=η1​+iy1​ηn​.(3.8)

4. Remove one momentum from the imaginary part

Smooth complex division. If a complex C∞C^\inftyC∞ function F(t,z)F(t,z)F(t,z), with real t,zt,zt,z, has F(0,0)=0F(0,0)=0F(0,0)=0 and ∂tF(0,0)≠0\partial_tF(0,0)\ne0∂t​F(0,0)=0, then every smooth G(t,z)G(t,z)G(t,z) has a representation

G=QF+S(z)(4.1) G=QF+S(z) \tag{4.1} G=QF+S(z)(4.1)

on a neighborhood chosen from FFF and the original domain, with Q,SQ,SQ,S smooth and complex valued. The remainder is independent of ttt. This is the k=1k=1k=1 case of Hörmander I, Theorem 7.5.6; its hypotheses are those of Theorem 7.5.5. Neither the quotient nor the remainder is asserted to be unique. The following proof treats complex functions in real variables; it does not assume that their real zeros form a parameter graph.

Proof. First extend a smooth function a(t,z)a(t,z)a(t,z) almost analytically in ttt. Multiply it by a fixed real cutoff equal to one on the patch in use. For v=t+iwv=t+iwv=t+iw, choose a fixed smooth cutoff χ\chiχ, equal to one near zero, and put

A(t+iw,z)=∑k=0∞χ(w/εk)(iw)kk!∂tka(t,z). A(t+iw,z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \chi(w/\varepsilon_k)\frac{(iw)^k}{k!}\partial_t^ka(t,z). A(t+iw,z)=k=0∑∞​χ(w/εk​)k!(iw)k​∂tk​a(t,z).

All coefficients and their derivatives are bounded on a fixed larger compact patch. A derivative of total order l<kl<kl<k of the kkk-th term is bounded by Cklεkk−lC_{kl}\varepsilon_k^{k-l}Ckl​εkk−l​. Choose positive radii decreasing to zero so that these bounds are at most 2−k2^{-k}2−k for every l≤k/2l\le k/2l≤k/2. Each fixed derivative series then converges uniformly after finitely many terms. The sum is smooth on a fixed complex domain; only the radii and its seminorm bounds depend on aaa. Its normal jets at w=0w=0w=0 are the formal analytic jets. Thus, with ∂vˉ=(∂t+i∂w)/2\partial_{\bar v}=(\partial_t+i\partial_w)/2∂vˉ​=(∂t​+i∂w​)/2, Taylor's integral remainder gives

A(t,z)=a(t,z),∣Dβ∂vˉA(t+iw,z)∣≤CβL∣w∣Lfor every β,L. A(t,z)=a(t,z),\qquad |D^\beta\partial_{\bar v}A(t+iw,z)|\le C_{\beta L}|w|^L \quad\text{for every }\beta,L. A(t,z)=a(t,z),∣Dβ∂vˉ​A(t+iw,z)∣≤CβL​∣w∣Lfor every β,L.

The derivatives here include all real parameters zzz. No holomorphic continuation of an arbitrary smooth function is claimed.

Apply this construction to FFF, writing its extension as F~(v,z)\widetilde F(v,z)F(v,z). At the mark, its real derivative in (t,w)(t,w)(t,w) is complex multiplication by λ=∂tF(0,0)≠0\lambda=\partial_tF(0,0)\ne0λ=∂t​F(0,0)=0. In particular it is invertible. A direct parameter argument produces a smooth complex root T(z)T(z)T(z), with T(0)=0T(0)=0T(0)=0. Indeed the real map

v⟼v−λ−1F~(v,z) v\longmapsto v-\lambda^{-1}\widetilde F(v,z) v⟼v−λ−1F(v,z)

has derivative zero at the mark. On a sufficiently small closed complex disc its derivative norm is at most q<1q<1q<1, uniformly on a smaller parameter patch. Shrink that patch so that its value at v=0v=0v=0 has modulus at most (1−q)/2(1-q)/2(1−q)/2 times the disc radius. It maps the disc into itself and its fixed point lies in the interior. Iteration from zero has geometrically summable successive differences, so completeness of C\mathbb CC gives its unique fixed point T(z)T(z)T(z). The same contraction estimate first bounds parameter differences of TTT by a constant times the parameter differences. Taylor's formula in the fixed-point identity then proves differentiability, with real derivative

DzT=−(DvF~(T,z))−1DzF~(T,z). D_zT=-(D_v\widetilde F(T,z))^{-1}D_z\widetilde F(T,z). Dz​T=−(Dv​F(T,z))−1Dz​F(T,z).

a0=P1+iP2p1+ip2=1+(ef1−1)p1+i(ef2−1)p2p1+ip2(8.16) a_0=\frac{P_1+iP_2}{p_1+ip_2} =1+\frac{(e^{f_1}-1)p_1+i(e^{f_2}-1)p_2}{p_1+ip_2} \tag{8.16} a0​=p1​+ip2​P1​+iP2​​=1+p1​+ip2​(ef1​−1)p1​+i(ef2​−1)p2​​(8.16)

extends smoothly and flatly from one across VVV. To justify division, use real normal coordinates (p1,p2,z)(p_1,p_2,z)(p1​,p2​,z) and r=(p12+p22)1/2r=(p_1^2+p_2^2)^{1/2}r=(p12​+p22​)1/2. A derivative of order lll of the reciprocal is O(r−1−l)O(r^{-1-l})O(r−1−l). Every derivative of the numerator is O(rN)O(r^N)O(rN) for arbitrary NNN, uniformly on a compact tangential patch. Leibniz gives an arbitrarily high power bound for every derivative of the quotient. Define those derivatives as zero on r=0r=0r=0; difference quotients and induction show that they are the actual continuous derivatives of the zero extension. Thus (8.16) is smooth, equals one on VVV, and is nonzero after shrinking. It has degree zero.

Finally P1,P2P_1,P_2P1​,P2​ have degree one, commute and have their Hamilton fields independent with RRR at the mark, because all preceding multipliers were nonzero and the flat corrections leave the fields there unchanged. The homogeneous coordinate-completion theorem makes them the first two momenta at (0,en)(0,e_n)(0,en​), using the unused last position index. Combining the preliminary degree change, eWe^WeW and a0a_0a0​ gives the multiplier in (8.2). □\square□

Exercise 12 (uniform smooth jets). Let Wj(r,z)W_j(r,z)Wj​(r,z) vanish to order jjj at r=0r=0r=0, with zzz in a fixed compact parameter patch. Explain how to choose radii in (8.11), and identify which normal jets of the sum are prescribed.

Solution. For each jjj and l≤j/2l\le j/2l≤j/2, Taylor's formula and the cutoff product rule give a finite bound Cj,lεj−lC_{j,l}\varepsilon^{j-l}Cj,l​εj−l for the ClC^lCl norm. At r=0r=0r=0, each cutoff is identically one near zero and terms with j>Nj>Nj>N have zero normal derivatives through order NNN. Therefore the sum's normal jet through order NNN is that of W0+⋯+WNW_0+\cdots+W_NW0​+⋯+WN​, with all parameter derivatives as well. No convergence of the uncut formal series is required.

Solution. On a compact parameter patch, Taylor's formula gives ∣DγN∣≤Cγ,M(s2+t2)M/2|D^\gamma N|\le C_{\gamma,M}(s^2+t^2)^{M/2}∣DγN∣≤Cγ,M​(s2+t2)M/2 for every MMM. Each derivative of order lll of (s+it)−1(s+it)^{-1}(s+it)−1 is bounded by Cl(s2+t2)−(1+l)/2C_l(s^2+t^2)^{-(1+l)/2}Cl​(s2+t2)−(1+l)/2. Every Leibniz term consequently has any desired positive power bound by choosing MMM large. All candidate derivatives extend continuously as zero. Inductively, their difference quotients in a normal direction tend to zero at the set, because one can use a power bound greater than one; tangential derivatives there are derivatives of the identically zero restriction. They are the true derivatives, proving smoothness and flatness. For N=sN=sN=s, the quotient is one along t=0,s≠0t=0,s\ne0t=0,s=0, and zero along s=0,t≠0s=0,t\ne0s=0,t=0, so it has no continuous extension.

Exercise 14 (involutive without an identically zero bracket). In dimension three let p=ex1+ix2(ξ1+iξ2)p=e^{x_1+i x_2}(\xi_1+i\xi_2)p=ex1​+ix2​(ξ1​+iξ2​), near (0,e3)(0,e_3)(0,e3​). Verify all hypotheses of Theorem 8.1 and give an exact multiplier.

Solution. The zero set is ξ1=ξ2=0\xi_1=\xi_2=0ξ1​=ξ2​=0, and at the mark its two real Hamilton fields are ∂x1,∂x2\partial_{x_1},\partial_{x_2}∂x1​​,∂x2​​, independent of R=∂ξ3R=\partial_{\xi_3}R=∂ξ3​​. More generally the coefficient matrix on VVV is the real matrix of multiplication by the nonzero complex number ex1+ix2e^{x_1+i x_2}ex1​+ix2​, hence invertible. Direct differentiation in both coordinate pairs gives

{p,pˉ}=−4ie2x1ξ2. \{p,\bar p\}=-4i e^{2x_1}\xi_2. {p,pˉ​}=−4ie2x1​ξ2​.

It vanishes on VVV, while it is nonzero at nearby points with ξ2≠0\xi_2\ne0ξ2​=0. The nonzero homogeneous degree-zero multiplier e−x1−ix2e^{-x_1-i x_2}e−x1​−ix2​ gives ξ1+iξ2\xi_1+i\xi_2ξ1​+iξ2​ exactly, with identity coordinates and the positive third-momentum mark. This example satisfies the source's on-zero-set bracket condition in its full intended scope.
